EHR-extracted information on body mass index (ie, BMI) levels can be used in conjunction with diagnosis-based models to enhance predictive models for utilization.
the addition of BMI information to risk adjustment models improves the ability to predict future costs and utilization.
the use of EHR-extracted information on body mass index (a measure of weight status) improved the performance of risk adjustment models to predict health care costs and use of medical services.

the use of EHR data to predict utilization.
developing and evaluating risk adjustment models using electronic health records.
the use of electronic health records (ERHs) in the development of predictive models of health care utilization and costs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of BMI data from EHRs can improve the prediction of utilization and cost, especially if comprehensive diagnostic information is missing.
the use of EHR-extracted data can be useful in improving the performance of risk-adjustment models.
BMI is a useful predictor of health care costs and use and can be used to augment risk-adjustment models.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
adding BMI to diagnosis-based models improves the prediction of utilization and costs, but only for models with limited diagnostic data.
BMI information can be used as a proxy to predict health service use and health care costs, especially when other clinical information such as diagnosis is unavailable or incomplete.
BMI is a useful predictor for cost and utilization, especially when combined with demographic information.
The main takeaway from our work is that
BMI is a useful addition to diagnosis-based models, but its impact on prediction is limited if comprehensive diagnostic data (eg, comorbidities) are present.
BMI can improve the performance of diagnosis-only models in predicting utilization and costs, but it cannot compensate for the absence of comprehensive diagnostic data.
the addition of BMI can enhance predictive models of cost, especially when the models are less comprehensive.
